title: 3D Printing Architecture
subtitle: Architecture prototype study pairing a printed spatial model with process animation
overview: 3D Printing Architecture presents a student work animation study about how a predesigned building could be assembled through crane-supported construction and 3D-printed cementitious concrete. The exhibit focuses on the model and its process animation: a compact way to read geometry, fabrication sequence and architectural intention together.
storyHtml:
This project uses model animation to simulate a construction method rather than to claim a finished building system. A crane and printing apparatus work around a predesigned architectural shell, placing 3D-printed cementitious concrete in a controlled sequence while prefab structural pieces and components are inserted where the printed material alone would not be enough.

The building process is organized around a 0.9-meter construction threshold. Each height band becomes a checkpoint: print the next layer set, stabilize the geometry, coordinate openings and services, then add selected prefab elements before the next stage begins. That rhythm turns the animation into a readable construction diagram instead of a simple object showcase.

The idea borrows from real 3D concrete printing research, where robotic arms, gantry systems and crane-mounted equipment can extrude material layer by layer from digital toolpaths. It also acknowledges the current practical limit of the technology: printed walls often still need reinforcement, post-installed parts, openings, fixtures and assembly logic to become architecture.

In Focus mode, the project should feel direct and process-led. The model establishes the designed form, while the animation explains how that form could be rapidly iterated and built through printed cement, staged thresholds and prefab coordination.
